title: Here come the floods: chemical priming of plant cysteine oxidases improves flood tolerance
content: Extreme weather events are an increasingly significant threat to global agriculture (FAO 2025). Flooding is one of the leading causes of crop losses worldwide, a problem expected to worsen as climate change increases both the frequency and intensity of extreme rainfall events. Unlike aquatic plants or certain flood-tolerant wetland species and varieties (eg deepwater rice), most crops are highly sensitive to flooding. They suffer rapidly from oxygen deprivation when soils become waterlogged or plants are submerged, severely limiting their growth, productivity, and ultimately, survival (Bailey-Serres and Colmer 2014). Plants can perceive oxygen availability through PLANT CYSTEINE OXIDASES (PCOs), enzymes that use molecular oxygen to oxidize and target specific transcription factors (TFs) for degradation via the N-degron pathway (Weits et al. 2014). Flooding-induced oxygen deprivation, or hypoxia, inactivates PCOs, allowing the accumulation of hypoxia-responsive TFs including GROUP VII ETHYLENE RESPONSE FACTORs (ERFVIIs). The latter initiate a transcriptional program that promotes survival. For example, ERFVIIs activate genes involved in ethanolic and lactic fermentation pathways (eg ALCOHOL DEHYDROGENASE [ADH]), thereby sustaining ATP production while regenerating NAD+ required to maintain glycolysis under anaerobic conditions (Gasch et al. 2016).
